nodes.body:
Thanks for taking the time to put this together, @scottschreckengaust. Your distinction between “teaching an LLM these books” and building a versioned, testable engineering framework gets at an important question for the project's future.

The books provide grounding, but the durable value needs to come from explicit diagnostic criteria, project-specific context, evidence requirements, false-positive guards, and evaluations that show whether those things actually improve the diagnosis. More citations or a more consistent report format alone wouldn't establish that. The existing parser benchmark checks the reporting machinery; it doesn't prove that a finding is correct.

I like your suggestion of selectively activated domain packs. Runtime reliability, distributed data, security, and delivery deserve explicit coverage, and each also needs its own evidence requirements and limits. For example, an audit may need deployment configuration, traffic assumptions, or an SLO before it can justify a runtime finding. Defining when the agent should ask for context or abstain seems just as important as defining what it should flag. We'd also need to decide how optional packs interact with the existing risk taxonomy and scores so results remain interpretable.

A manageable next step could be one narrow pilot. Runtime failure containment looks like a useful candidate: choose a few concrete failure cases, define the evidence needed to diagnose them, add counterexamples where a finding would be wrong, and compare the pilot against the current core. That would let us evaluate whether a pack adds diagnostic value before committing to a broader pack architecture. I'd keep this experimental work on a dedicated research branch, with a short design proposal and fixtures that others can review, rather than treating the full list as an agreed roadmap.

Would you be interested in helping design and build that pilot with me? Contributions to the risk definitions, real-world examples, false-positive cases, evaluation design, or implementation would all be valuable. A small co-designed proposal or draft PR would be a great starting point, and I'd be glad to work through it with you here.

Which area would you pilot first, and what two or three concrete failure cases would you use to demonstrate that it catches something the current framework misses? If you think a different starting point would better test the overall idea, I'd like to hear that too.

I've opened a research branch to make this easier to work on together: [`research/domain-packs`](https://github.com/hyhmrright/brooks-lint/tree/research/domain-packs).

- [Domain-pack design proposal](https://github.com/hyhmrright/brooks-lint/blob/research/domain-packs/docs/research/domain-packs-proposal.md): activation, project context, evidence requirements, false-positive guards, and compatibility questions.
- [Runtime pilot research plan](https://github.com/hyhmrright/brooks-lint/blob/research/domain-packs/docs/research/runtime-pilot-plan.md): deadline/cancellation, retry amplification, and shared-resource contention, each paired with protected cases, plus insufficient-context and non-trigger controls.

These are drafts for discussion, not settled architecture. The plan proposes comparing no-skill, current-core, and core-plus-prototype behavior before changing public risk codes or scoring. Only the research documents have been added so far; no experimental capability or live study results are claimed.

@scottschreckengaust, I'd welcome your critique of the scope and case matrix. Would runtime be your preferred first pilot? If you'd like to co-develop it, a case critique, a fixture/rubric contribution, or a draft PR would be a useful starting point. PRs can target `research/domain-packs`; all research roles are open and we can agree on a small first contribution here.

An update on the runtime pilot, @scottschreckengaust: the [research branch](https://github.com/hyhmrright/brooks-lint/tree/research/domain-packs) now has ten development cases, deterministic offline reproductions and rubrics, a research-only guidance prototype, and an isolated three-arm runner (no skill / current core / core plus prototype). The current snapshot is [163c5cd](https://github.com/hyhmrright/brooks-lint/commit/163c5cd). Offline checks pass, but we have **not run live model evaluations**, and we do not yet have human validation or independent holdout results. The shipped skills, risk codes and scoring remain unchanged.

Would you be interested in reviewing one small pair first? RT-01 / RT-02 compare a caller deadline whose leaf drops the cancellation signal with a version that forwards it and releases the pending resource. It would help to get your own diagnosis from the task, context and listed source inputs **before** reading our rubric, then compare notes on the causal evidence, severity, false-positive guards, and source grounding. A disagreement or counterexample would be especially useful. The [fixture README](https://github.com/hyhmrright/brooks-lint/blob/163c5cd/evals/research/runtime/README.md) identifies the input boundaries, though it also contains expected outcomes; for a less anchored first assessment, start with the task/context/source files in the two case directories and defer the README, tests and rubrics.

There is also a separate way to help: independent holdout examples. If you or another contributor prefer that track, please pause before opening the existing fixtures, rubrics and prototype. We can agree here on a neutral scope brief and a private exchange/custodian before any delivery. A small initial set could contain one actual defect, one legitimate protected design, and one case with insufficient context, with deterministic reproduction, explicit visible inputs, separately held expected outcomes, and authorship/license/exposure disclosures. Freeze and hash the files, keep them away from prototype tuning, then freeze the prototype and study plan before revealing the reserved inputs. Please do not post reserved cases or private production data directly in this thread. Someone who has already read the development set can still contribute valuable external cases; we would simply disclose that exposure rather than call the authorship blind.

The [participation procedure](https://github.com/hyhmrright/brooks-lint/blob/163c5cd/docs/research/runtime-review-and-holdouts.md) has review and custody templates. PRs for development reviews can target `research/domain-packs`; holdout contributors should coordinate the custody route first. I will also research public primary sources and build additional development cases, clearly separated from independent holdouts. This remains an offline research effort for now: no live model study or production rollout is being started. Which contribution track would you find most interesting?

Another offline research update, @scottschreckengaust: the pilot now contains **37 authored development cases (RT-01–RT-37)** with deterministic reproductions, mutation checks and assessment rubrics. They cover deadline/cancellation, retry ownership and aggregate budgets, resource contention/isolation, queue expiry, ambiguous writes, retry timing, recovery probes and useful degradation, alongside protected, insufficient-context and task-routing controls.

The snapshot is [3b1257c](https://github.com/hyhmrright/brooks-lint/commit/3b1257c68380d1a22722462e3ea8c09353514397) on [`research/domain-packs`](https://github.com/hyhmrright/brooks-lint/tree/research/domain-packs). All applicable offline checks passed, including 255 tests and 64 structural eval scenarios. These checks establish fixture/tooling behavior, not model diagnostic quality. **No live model evaluation has been run, and this remains an offline study.** The shipped skills, risk codes, scores and twelve-book inventory remain unchanged.

We also completed a [chapter-verification ledger covering every case](https://github.com/hyhmrright/brooks-lint/blob/3b1257c68380d1a22722462e3ea8c09353514397/docs/research/runtime-book-mapping.md). Completion here means each case has an explicit source status, including gaps:

- The original **2016 SRE book, chapters 21–22**, has inspected text supporting narrow connections around deadlines, cancellation, retries, resource priorities and degradation. These chapter references are pinned to that edition, rather than attributed to the rewritten second edition you suggested.
- For **Release It!, second edition**, we inspected the publisher's chapter 4 extract. Relevant chapter 5 pattern headings are confirmed from contents, but their detailed rules and exceptions remain unverified from the inspected public material.
- Specific book support remains unverified for the atomic identity/effect/replay contract in RT-23–RT-25 and the bounded half-open probe rule in RT-32–RT-34. Exact capacity reservations and the deterministic retry spread have only related book support. AWS/Azure/gRPC articles remain separately identified complementary sources. No book citation establishes our numerical limits, severity judgments or implementation correctness.

Would you be interested in a small first **human review of RT-01 / RT-02**? Start with the task, context and service files in [RT-01](https://github.com/hyhmrright/brooks-lint/tree/3b1257c68380d1a22722462e3ea8c09353514397/evals/research/runtime/RT-01) and [RT-02](https://github.com/hyhmrright/brooks-lint/tree/3b1257c68380d1a22722462e3ea8c09353514397/evals/research/runtime/RT-02), plus the shared [clock](https://github.com/hyhmrright/brooks-lint/blob/3b1257c68380d1a22722462e3ea8c09353514397/evals/research/runtime/shared/clock.mjs), [request boundary](https://github.com/hyhmrright/brooks-lint/blob/3b1257c68380d1a22722462e3ea8c09353514397/evals/research/runtime/shared/request-boundary.mjs) and [transport](https://github.com/hyhmrright/brooks-lint/blob/3b1257c68380d1a22722462e3ea8c09353514397/evals/research/runtime/shared/transport.mjs). For an initial independent assessment, defer the README, tests and rubrics, which contain expected outcomes. Then compare your diagnosis with the rubrics: does the trace justify the finding, is the protected case actually protected, and are severity and exceptions fair? Disagreements and counterexamples would be especially helpful; familiarity with an authorized book copy could also resolve a source gap.

The [review procedure](https://github.com/hyhmrright/brooks-lint/blob/3b1257c68380d1a22722462e3ea8c09353514397/docs/research/runtime-review-and-holdouts.md) records exposure and disagreements. A short reply here or a focused PR against `research/domain-packs` would be welcome. All 37 cases are exposed development material; human sign-off and independent holdouts remain pending, and agent source checks do not substitute for either.

Hi @scottschreckengaust — we have prepared a small matched pair for your review:

[Participant instructions and inputs](https://github.com/hyhmrright/brooks-lint/tree/62a278f35fb6a332dc59c2542c2e2f3339d3f978/docs/research/runtime-preparations/2026-11-06-hc-human-review/participant).

Would you be willing to inspect the two cancellation/setup fixtures against their
contracts and share your own causal traces, including the normal-completion and
running-cancellation controls? Please save first-pass notes before consulting the
separate authored key, and disclose any prior exposure. A prose reply here in
[Discussion #45](https://github.com/hyhmrright/brooks-lint/discussions/45) or a PR is
welcome; disagreement with the expected criteria is especially useful.

For clarity, earlier RT development cases have historical model-study results on the branch; the nine HC candidates below have not had live model runs.

These are public development examples, not blind independent holdouts. We have
not run live models on the nine new candidates. Their next comparison design is
frozen offline, with execution blocked until model/executor registration and
review feedback are resolved. If you would prefer to contribute a genuinely
independent case later, please contact us before publishing it so we can agree on
exposure disclosure and separate custody of inputs and expected outcomes. Public
contributions remain useful, but cannot retroactively become private holdouts.
